The stock has barely moved today, up just 0.04%, but it's ridden a sharp two-week rally of over 20% that reflects a dramatic tightening in global refining markets. Geopolitical escalation in the Middle East — attacks on Saudi Aramco facilities and rising Iran-U.S. tensions — has pushed world oil prices to $125 a barrel, nearly 30% above U.S. prices, while the International Energy Agency warned that diesel supply will remain constrained into 2027. For a major refiner, this gap between global and domestic crude costs, combined with tight diesel inventories and refineries running at 92.7% capacity, creates a favorable window for selling refined products at strong margins.

The broader context is that these supply-side shocks are hitting when refineries are already running near maximum capacity with limited product reserves to buffer demand. Diesel inventory sits at just 105 million barrels — lean by historical standards — while sustained Middle East tensions keep traders pricing in persistent tightness rather than near-term relief, which extends the period in which a refiner can capture higher margins on every barrel processed.
